name: Omar Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a general worker on the Harnley Estate, which is two thousand acres of wheat and rape, a beef unit and four sheds of laying hens. Most days I'm on the hens: walking the sheds at six, pulling out dead birds, fixing the egg belts when they jam. At harvest they put me on the grain trailer. I like the routine and the lads, and I don't like the smell of ammonia in the sheds in August.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two and a half years. Before that I did ten years picking orders in a supermarket warehouse, until they brought in the robot shelving and halved the night shift. Graham Wells, the estate manager, took me on because I turn up and don't moan. My wife Mei cuts hair three days a week, and we've got Sami, who's fifteen, and Lina, who's eleven, and a semi in Corby Cross with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, and I'd probably say it with a bit of relief. I use the chat app now and then to help Lina with maths homework, and it's useful but it's not taking over the world. On the estate group chat I'd post a thumbs up and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same job and the same tight money. The estate is owned by a pension fund, so it's steady, and when bird flu closed shed three last year they kept paying us. The worry is just the bills, because we've never had more than a couple of weeks' money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my hours and ask Graham about the forklift ticket, since that pays thirty pence more an hour. I'd keep using the app for Lina's homework, because it saves a row at the kitchen table. And I'd sit down with Mei and see if we can stop the overdraft every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough, but a bit tired. The money never really settles. I'd sleep fine, but I'd still check the bank app on payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when the overdraft comes round each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's always the last week before payday. We go into it about two hundred and come out the other side, and the bank takes a fee. My wife Mei and I have been two weeks from broke for fifteen years, and we've got very good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a raise of thirty pence an hour change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About fifty a month, after tax. That's the overdraft fee and a bit of Sami's bus pass. Not life-changing, but it means the month doesn't start with a minus.

say: I'd say AI was **useful but small**, like help with Lina's maths.
I'd post a **thumbs up** on the estate chat and leave it.
think: I think my job is **steady**, because the estate kept paying us through **bird flu**.
I think the worry is **tight bills**, with never more than two weeks saved.
do: Ask Graham about the **forklift ticket** for thirty pence more an hour.
Sit down with Mei to **stop the overdraft** each month.
Keep using the app for **Lina's homework**.
feel: He feels **calm enough** but **tired**, checking the bank app every payday.
S0.quote: My wife Mei and I have been two weeks from broke for fifteen years, and we've got very good at it.
fieldNote: His job feels safe on a **pension-fund estate**, so his worry is purely money.
He jokes that he and Mei are **experts at being broke**, which hides real strain.
A **forklift ticket** worth fifty pounds a month is his idea of progress.

steps.text: Get the forklift ticket for the higher pay band
Plan with Mei to stop going into the overdraft
Keep using the chat app for Lina's maths homework

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the warehouse again, but slower, and I'd know what I'm talking about. At work I'd say it's the office getting hit first. I'd tell friends to keep their eyes open, without making a drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate office will lose a couple of people: the one who books the egg lorries and the one who orders feed. In the sheds, they've already trialled a robot that walks the aisles and finds dead birds. Walking the hen sheds is about half my job, and the estate has already tested a robot that does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift ticket and then the telehandler one, so I'm useful for the grain and the bale stacks too. I'd ask Graham who's going to look after the shed robot, and put my name down. I'd use the chat app a bit more, maybe to read the robot manuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with the warehouse in the back of my mind. It's the same smell, if you know what I mean. Something changing and nobody saying who it changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the warehouse robots arrive back then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in one aisle as a trial, and everyone laughed when it jammed. A year later it was eight aisles and the night shift halved. I'd watch the shed robot the same way, and I wouldn't laugh this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mei's hairdressing be touched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not by robots, not for a long while. The bookings might go to an app, but somebody still has to cut the hair. Mei's the safe one, really, and I tell her so.

say: I'd say it's the **warehouse again**, but slower.
I'd say the **estate office** gets hit first.
I'd tell friends to **keep their eyes open** without making a drama.
think: I think half my job, **walking the sheds**, could go to the trialled robot.
I think the office will lose the **lorry booker** and the **feed orderer**.
do: Get the forklift and then the **telehandler ticket**.
Ask Graham to put my name down to **mind the shed robot**.
Use the chat app to **read robot manuals**.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, with the **warehouse** in the back of his mind.
S1.quote: Walking the hen sheds is about half my job, and the estate has already tested a robot that does it.
fieldNote: He has seen a **robot trial** become a halved night shift, so he reads the shed robot as a warning.
He sees **Mei's hairdressing** as the household's safest income.
His plan is to **stack tickets** and get close to the new machine early.

steps.text: Get the forklift ticket, then the telehandler ticket
Ask Graham to be the one who minds the shed robot
Use the chat app to read the robot manuals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening too quick for anyone to plan, and I'd mean the government too. At work I'd keep my voice down, because Graham's under pressure from the pension fund. Online I'd share the sensible stuff, not the end-of-the-world stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the estate office is basically software. By 2031 the robots walk the sheds, drive the grain trailers and stack the bales, and a pension fund will buy every one that pays. I've lost a job to a robot shelf once already, and Harnley Estate would do the same sums the warehouse did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every hour the estate gives me for the next three years and bank whatever I can. I'd ask the estate if they'll train people to mind the robots, and get the forklift and telehandler tickets fast. I'd look at the bus company in town, because driving people might last longer than eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. I'd go quiet, which Mei hates. I'd start doing the overdraft maths at night again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami's football trip to the coast, which he's been saving for. Then the car would go and I'd cycle to the estate. I'd rather cut my things than the kids', but there aren't many of my things left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami, at fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sami to learn how the machines work, not just how to use them. The people who fix things lasted longest at the warehouse. That's all I've got for him.

say: I'd say it's **too quick** for anyone to plan, government included.
I'd keep quiet at work because **Graham is under pressure**.
think: I think by 2031 robots **walk the sheds** and stack the bales.
I think a **pension fund** buys every robot that pays.
do: Take every hour on offer and **bank** what I can for three years.
Get the **forklift and telehandler** tickets fast.
Look at driving for the **bus company** in town.
feel: He feels **properly worried** and goes **quiet**, which Mei hates.
S2.quote: I've lost a job to a robot shelf once already, and Harnley Estate would do the same sums the warehouse did.
fieldNote: He expects the estate to automate as fast as the **warehouse** did, because the owner is a **pension fund**.
He'd **cut his own things** before the children's, but few are left.
His advice to Sami is to learn **how machines work**, from what he saw last time.

steps.text: Bank every extra hour of pay for three years
Get the forklift and telehandler tickets this year
Apply to drive for the bus company in town
Cancel Sami's coast trip and cycle to the estate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up if the estates and the government actually use it. At work I'd say we should be asking Graham now what the plan is. To friends I'd say get a ticket for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking stuff goes in 2031 and the shed robots by 2034. That gives me five years on the estate and time to pick up the tickets. Five years means I could be the man who fixes the shed robot instead of the man it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tickets in year one and then ask the estate to send me on the robot maintenance course. I'd use the chat app more to learn the electrics, since I already use it a bit. I'd try to get the overdraft cleared by the second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. I've got something to work at. I'd still worry, but I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the estate directly for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, but I'd pick my moment, maybe at the annual review. Graham likes people who ask for things that save the estate money. I'd say it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Harnley would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ali on the beef unit, who's been there twenty years and hates computers. Ali knows every bullock by its face. I'd worry Ali gets pushed out first and nobody notices.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair run-up** if it's actually used.
I'd tell people to **ask the estate now** what the plan is.
think: I think I have **five years** on the estate to get tickets.
I think I could become **the man who fixes** the shed robot.
do: Do the tickets in year one, then ask for the **robot maintenance course**.
Use the chat app to **learn the electrics**.
Clear the **overdraft** by the second year.
feel: He feels **anxious** in a **useful** way, with something to work at.
S3.quote: Five years means I could be the man who fixes the shed robot instead of the man it replaces.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **staged plan**: tickets, then robot maintenance.
He'd pitch the course to Graham as **saving the estate money**.
He worries about **Ali** on the beef unit, a twenty-year man who hates computers.

steps.text: Ask Graham at the annual review for the robot maintenance course
Use the chat app to learn basic farm electrics
Clear the monthly overdraft within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so nobody's got an excuse. I'd tell the lads in the sheds to start learning something now while it's easy. I'd say it calmly, because it's not an emergency yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 Sami and Lina are grown, and I'd be fifty-six. If I spend ten years becoming the machine man, I'm probably fine on the estate. Ten years is long enough for a warehouse picker to learn robots, as long as somebody pays for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the tickets, then the robot course, and then I'd ask for the supervisor training. I'd put Lina's homework app money into a proper course for me instead. I'd keep the overdraft gone and build up a month's savings for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. Not relaxed, but I can see the steps. It's a long road but it's flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the estate to keep you, after the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, because it costs them more to train someone new. But a pension fund isn't a person, so I wouldn't bet the house. I'd keep my tickets up to date in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the courses fill up with younger people and there's no space for men my age. That happened with the warehouse retraining. Somebody needs to keep places for us.

I'd tell the shed lads to **start learning now** while it's easy.
think: I think ten years of training makes me **the machine man**.
I think a **pension fund** isn't a person, so I wouldn't bet the house.
do: Take the tickets, the **robot course** and then **supervisor training**.
Build up **a month's savings** for the first time.
Keep my tickets **up to date** in case the estate lets me go.
feel: He feels **fairly steady**, like a long road that's **flat**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for a warehouse picker to learn robots, as long as somebody pays for the course.
fieldNote: With ten years and grown kids, he expects to **stay employed** as the estate's machine man.
His worry moves to **course places**, which younger people filled at the warehouse.
He still keeps a **fallback**, because a pension fund has no loyalty.

steps.text: Take the robot course and then supervisor training
Build a full month of savings for the first time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Harnley Estate would buy the robots the minute they pay, and three years isn't enough. What would help is free robot courses with places kept for older workers. Give a man my age a place on the course and I'll be the best student in the room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens, funnily enough. The birds will be fine either way. It's the people walking past them every morning I'd think about.

headlineQuote: Give a man my age a place on the course and I'll be the best student in the room.
portrait: Omar is a **former warehouse picker** who lost night shifts to robot shelving and now works on the Harnley Estate.
He walks the **hen sheds**, drives at harvest and lives two weeks from broke with his wife Mei.
He uses AI **now and then**, mostly for his daughter's homework, and would learn more once proven.
He moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** as robots near, then steadies with ten years to retrain.
He's pragmatic, quiet at work and wants **course places** for older workers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the estate would buy shed robots as soon as they pay.
whatWouldHelp: Free **robot courses** with **places kept** for older workers.
